bai.moTa: The spatial part of curvature: Flamm’s paraboloid, rulers longer than the difference in radii
bai.yChinh: Around a mass, the circumference of a circle is still $2\pi r$, but the distance measured with a ruler between two circles is **longer** than the difference of their radii: $\dd\ell = \dd r/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$. The curved surface in the picture (Flamm’s paraboloid) is an “all at the same moment” slice through the equator, embedded in three-dimensional space so that the extra length becomes visible. It is the **spatial** part of curvature; the time part (Lesson 9 and Lesson 10) is what mainly makes things fall.
bai.giaiThich:
- The curved surface is an **“all at the same moment” slice** ($t$ = constant) through the equatorial plane of the space around a mass, embedded in an imaginary three-dimensional space. The vertical direction is only for drawing; it is not real.
- $r$ is defined through circumference: the circle has circumference $2\pi r$. But the true distance in the radial direction is $\dd\ell = \dd r/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$, longer than $\dd r$.
- The extra length: Earth 3.1 mm over 6,371 km; Sun 1.02 km over 695,700 km; neutron star 1.78 km over 12 km.
- Outside is Flamm’s paraboloid $z = 2\sqrt{r_s(r - r_s)}$; inside a star of uniform density it is a spherical cap.
- Curved space contributes half of the bending of light, but has almost no effect on slow objects (of order $(v/c)^2$ compared with the time part).
- The picture of “a rubber sheet with a marble rolling on it” is misleading: Flamm’s paraboloid has no “downward,” it is not a funnel for things to roll into, and it leaves out the time part.
bai.conSo.1: **3.1 mm**: going from the ground up to the circle of twice the radius (another 6,371 km), a ruler measures this much more than flat geometry predicts.
bai.conSo.2: **1.02 km** over 695,700 km: the same kind of extra length around the Sun. From the Sun’s surface to Earth’s orbit: 7.9 km.
bai.conSo.3: **About 15%**: the extra length around a neutron star (1.78 km over 12 km). Space there is visibly curved.
bai.conSo.4: **8/9**: no star can stay at rest if it is compressed beyond this point (a radius smaller than 9/8 of its Schwarzschild radius); it must collapse into a black hole.
bai.conSo.5: **Of order 10⁻⁸**: the contribution of curved space to Earth’s orbit, compared with the time part.
bai.hieuDung: **This mesh is not a “rubber sheet” with a ball pressing it down.** The rubber-sheet picture suggests that objects roll into the dip because gravity pulls them, which uses gravity to explain gravity. Flamm’s paraboloid is just a map of distances in space at one moment; it has no “downward.” An apple falls mainly because *time* runs more slowly close to the ground (Lesson 9 and Lesson 10), not because space has a dip.
bai.nguon: Exterior and interior Schwarzschild solutions (1916); Flamm’s embedding (1916); Hartle 2003, chapters 6, 7, 9. Neutron star taken at a typical 1.4 solar masses, radius 12 km. Every extra distance recomputed from CODATA 2018 and IAU constants; see kiem-tra/kiem-phan-3-cu.mjs.

bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Distinguish the radius defined through circumference from the distance measured with a ruler in the radial direction.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Compute the true distance between two spheres around Earth, the Sun and a neutron star.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Explain why curved space contributes half of the bending of light but has almost no effect on slow objects.

bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: What this curved surface is: a slice of space
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Lesson 9 and Lesson 10 dealt with the **time** part of curvature: clocks lower down run slow, and that is what makes things fall. This lesson deals with the rest: the shape of **space** around a mass.

The mesh you see is built like this:

1. Take the four-dimensional spacetime around a star.
2. Pick **one moment** $t$ of an observer very far away: an “all at the same moment” slice, like the “now” sheet in Lesson 4. What remains is three-dimensional space.
3. Keep only the **equatorial plane** through the star’s center. What remains is a two-dimensional surface.

That two-dimensional surface is curved. To see the curvature, we “embed” it in an imaginary three-dimensional space so that distances measured along the surface equal the true distances. The colored part in the middle is the star’s matter; the white ring is the star’s surface.

> [Lưu ý] The picture has dropped the time dimension and one space dimension. **The vertical direction (the purple arrow) is only for drawing**; it is not a real dimension of the universe. What is real is distance measured along the surface.

> [Thử ngay] The sphere in the middle is the star drawn in three dimensions so you can recognize it; on the slice, the star itself is the colored part, and the sphere’s equator lies exactly on the white ring. Hover over the sphere to see its data.
> [[Side view|ngang]] [[View from above|tren]] [[Full view|tong]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Seen from above, the mesh is just ordinary concentric circles. That is what a two-dimensional creature living on this surface sees as it walks around the star: the circles have circumferences
$2\pi \times 1$, $2\pi \times 2$, …, $2\pi \times 6$ (in units of the star’s radius).

Around a mass, the $r$ of a circle is **defined** by measuring its circumference and dividing by $2\pi$. This can be measured from outside: you only need to stretch a string around the star. You cannot push a ruler into the center of a star, let alone a black hole. This quantity $r$ is sometimes called the {{bán kính chu vi|reduced circumference}}; it is exactly the $r$ in the clock-rate formula of Lesson 9.

In flat space, two circles with circumferences $2\pi \times 1$ and $2\pi \times 2$ must be exactly **1 unit** apart. The question of this lesson: around a mass, is that still true?

> [Thử ngay] Look from the side to see that these circles actually sit at different heights on a curved surface.
> [[View from above|tren]] [[Side view|ngang]] [[Full view|tong]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: The ruler measures more than the difference in radii
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
It is not. The **white** ruler lies along the surface, with marks 0.5 units apart as measured by the ruler. The **blue** ruler beside it marks where the ticks would sit if space were flat (0.5 apart in the difference of radii). The white marks fall behind the blue ones: between two circles there is **more ruler** than the difference in radii.

For the neutron star in the picture, from the surface (circle 1) to circle 2 the ruler measures **1.148 units** instead of 1: almost 15% extra. The general rule for a short radial segment:

$$ \dd\ell = \frac{\dd r}{\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}} $$

- $\dd r$: the difference of two “reduced circumferences”;
- $\dd\ell$: the {{khoảng cách riêng|proper distance}}, measured with a ruler at rest right there.

The closer to the mass, the larger the factor $1/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$: at the surface of the neutron star it is 1.235; at $r = 2\,r_s$ around a black hole it is 1.414. That is why the mesh has to slope down toward the center: the sloping part holds the extra length.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the two white dots at the ends of the ruler, right on the curved surface: the label at the end of the ruler shows the length measured by the ruler $\ell$ and the difference of radii $\Delta r$. Each time the white ruler passes a mark there is a high “tick,” and for the blue ruler a low “tick.” Drag the outer end outward starting next to the star: the high ticks come faster than the low ones, and that is the extra length (the sound is only an illustration, not a real sound).
> [[Neutron star|nt]] [[More compressed (rs/R = 0.6)|nen6]] [[Black hole|ld]] [[Close-up of the ruler|gan]]

+++ Go deeper: getting the formula from the Schwarzschild metric
The Schwarzschild metric (Lesson 9) is

$$ \dd s^2 = -\left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2\dd t^2 + \frac{\dd r^2}{1 - r_s/r} + r^2\left(\dd\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dd\phi^2\right). $$

The “all at the same moment” slice has $\dd t = 0$; the equatorial plane has $\theta = 90°$, $\dd\theta = 0$. What remains is the geometry of a two-dimensional surface:

$$ \dd\ell^2 = \frac{\dd r^2}{1 - r_s/r} + r^2\,\dd\phi^2. $$

- Going around ($\dd r = 0$): $\dd\ell = r\,\dd\phi$, so the circumference is $2\pi r$, just as defined.
- Going radially ($\dd\phi = 0$): $\dd\ell = \dd r/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$.

Integrating from $r_1$ to $r_2$ (both outside the mass):

$$ \ell = \Big[\sqrt{r(r - r_s)} + r_s \ln\!\left(\sqrt{r} + \sqrt{r - r_s}\right)\Big]_{r_1}^{r_2}. $$

The model uses exactly this formula for the readout, and places each ruler mark by adding up $\dd\ell$ in very small steps.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: For the **neutron star**, put the inner end of the ruler against the surface (the white ring), then drag the outer end until the ruler reads exactly **2.00 units** (within 0.03). Look at the label at the end of the ruler: what is the difference in radii then?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: The inner end snaps onto the white ring when you drag it close. When the ruler reads 2.00, the difference in radii is only about 1.79: more than 0.2 units of length lie in the steep part of the surface near the star.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Plugging in numbers: Earth, the Sun, a neutron star
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Choose each object in the control panel or press the buttons below. The readout in the lower left shows the real extra length. For ordinary objects the extra length is so small that the mesh would look almost perfectly flat, so the model **exaggerates the dip** (the readout says by how much).

| Measured radially | Difference in radii | Ruler longer by |
|---|---|---|
| Earth: from the ground up to $r = 2R$ | 6,371 km | 3.1 mm |
| Sun: from the surface up to $r = 2R$ | 695,700 km | 1.02 km |
| From the Sun’s surface to Earth’s orbit | 149.6 million km | 7.9 km |
| Neutron star: from the surface up to $r = 2R$ | 12 km | 1.78 km |
| Black hole: from the horizon up to $r = 2\,r_s$ | $r_s$ | an extra 1.30 $r_s$ |

When the field is weak ($r_s \ll r$), the extra length has a neat formula:

$$ \Delta\ell - (r_2 - r_1) \approx \frac{r_s}{2}\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}. $$

For Earth $r_s = 8{,}87$ mm and $r_2/r_1 = 2$: extra length $\approx 4{,}43\ \text{mm} \times 0{,}693 \approx 3{,}1$ mm.

> [Con số] The curvature of space around the Sun makes the true distance from the Sun’s surface to Earth’s orbit about 7.9 km longer than the difference in radii, out of a total of 149.6 million km: about five parts in a hundred million.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the pink dot on the “Compression” scale to the left of the scene: up is a diffuse object (Earth), down is a dense one (neutron star), and at the very bottom a black hole. Passing each object rings a bell, deeper for denser objects.
> [[Earth|dat]] [[Sun|mt]] [[Neutron star|nt]] [[Black hole|ld]]

+++ Go deeper: the weak-field formula
When $r_s/r$ is small, $1/\sqrt{1 - x} \approx 1 + x/2$, so

$$ \dd\ell \approx \left(1 + \frac{r_s}{2r}\right)\dd r \ \Rightarrow\ \ell \approx (r_2 - r_1) + \frac{r_s}{2}\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}. $$

For the Sun ($r_s = 2{,}95$ km) going from the surface ($695\,700$ km) to 1 AU: $\ln(149{,}6 \times 10^6 / 695\,700) \approx 5{,}37$, extra length $\approx 1{,}48\ \text{km} \times 5{,}37 \approx 7{,}9$ km.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the “Compression” scale (or the slider) to the density at which, from the surface up to circle 2, the ruler is exactly **10%** longer than the difference in radii (the readout “From circle 1 to circle 2” shows 1.100, within 0.005).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The extra length lies between the Sun (almost 0) and the neutron star (14.8%). The density you need is about 0.25: a star only 4 times its own Schwarzschild radius.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Flamm’s paraboloid: the true shape of the slice
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Which embedded surface holds exactly that extra length? In 1916, right after Schwarzschild found his solution, Ludwig Flamm worked out the answer: outside the mass, the embedded surface has height

$$ z(r) = 2\sqrt{r_s\,(r - r_s)}. $$

It is a **paraboloid** lying on its side ({{mặt Flamm|Flamm’s paraboloid}}). Near the mass it is steep; farther out it levels off but never becomes completely flat: the slope falls off like $\sqrt{r_s/r}$.

For a black hole, Flamm’s paraboloid goes all the way down to $r = r_s$, where it becomes **vertical**: that is the narrow throat at the event horizon. From the horizon out to the circle of circumference $2\pi \times 2\,r_s$, a ruler measures 2.30 $r_s$, not 1.

> [Lưu ý] For a black hole, the picture shows only the region outside the horizon. An “all at the same moment” slice according to faraway clocks cannot reach inside the horizon; Lesson 16 uses a different kind of drawing for that region.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the two ends of the ruler on the black hole’s Flamm paraboloid. Put the inner end right at the horizon: the first stretch is vertical, so the ruler reading shoots up while the difference in radii barely moves.
> [[Black hole, side view|ldNgang]] [[Neutron star|nt]] [[Full view|tong]]

+++ Go deeper: deriving Flamm’s paraboloid
Place a surface of revolution $z(r)$ in flat three-dimensional space with cylindrical coordinates $(r;\ \phi;\ z)$. Distance on the surface:

$$ \dd\ell^2 = \dd r^2 + \dd z^2 + r^2\dd\phi^2 = \left(1 + z'^2\right)\dd r^2 + r^2\dd\phi^2. $$

To match the Schwarzschild slice $\dd\ell^2 = \dd r^2/(1 - r_s/r) + r^2\dd\phi^2$, we need

$$ 1 + z'^2 = \frac{1}{1 - r_s/r} \ \Rightarrow\ z'^2 = \frac{r_s}{r - r_s} \ \Rightarrow\ z' = \sqrt{\frac{r_s}{r - r_s}}. $$

Integrating: $z = 2\sqrt{r_s(r - r_s)}$, that is $r = r_s + z^2/(4r_s)$: a parabola rotated about the vertical axis. For example $z(2\,r_s) = 2\,r_s$, $z(5\,r_s) = 4\,r_s$. All of the extra length lies in the slope $z'$; the part far from the center is gentle, so it adds almost nothing.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: For the **black hole**, drag the two ends of the ruler so that the ruler is **twice** the difference in radii: $\ell / \Delta r = 2{,}00$ (within 0.05), with $\Delta r$ at least 1 $r_s$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Put the inner end right at the horizon: the extra length is all packed into the vertical stretch there. From the horizon out to $r = 2\,r_s$ the ratio is 2.30; out to $r = 5\,r_s$ it is only 1.48. The target is around $r \approx 2{,}45\,r_s$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: Inside the star: a spherical cap
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Flamm’s paraboloid is only correct outside the mass. Inside the star, the deeper you go the less mass lies inside the circle, so the curvature changes. For a star of **uniform density** (a simple model that Schwarzschild also solved in 1916), the slice inside is a **spherical cap** of radius

$$ A = \sqrt{\frac{R^3}{r_s}}, $$

joining smoothly onto Flamm’s paraboloid at the star’s surface. The colored part in the picture is that cap. For the neutron star in the picture, $A \approx 1{,}70\,R$.

Drag the **Compress object** slider to the right: the same mass is squeezed into a smaller and smaller radius, and the cap gets deeper. There is a limit: once $r_s/R$ exceeds $8/9$ (that is, $R < \tfrac98 r_s$), no static star can hold itself up, because the pressure at the center would have to be infinite to resist the compression. Such a star must collapse into a black hole. That is why the slider stops at 0.86.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the pink dot on the “Compression” scale gradually downward and look from the side: the cap deepens and the edge of the star gets steeper. The readout shows the slope at the star’s edge.
> [[White dwarf|lt]] [[Neutron star|nt]] [[Compressed close to the limit (0.86)|max]] [[Side view|ngang]]

> [Lưu ý] Real neutron stars do not have uniform density; the cap here is an illustrative model. The outside part (Flamm’s paraboloid) is correct for every non-rotating spherical star.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Compress the star until the curved surface at its edge slopes at exactly **45°** (within about 1°). Then, right at the surface, the ruler measures $\sqrt2 \approx 1{,}414$ times the difference in radii.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The slope at the edge is $\tan\theta = \sqrt{C/(1 - C)}$ with $C = r_s/R$. A 45° slope means $\tan\theta = 1$, so $C = 0{,}5$: the star’s radius is exactly twice its Schwarzschild radius.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
This step adds color by clock rate (exaggerated so it is easy to see; yellow is where clocks run noticeably slow): that is the **time** part from Lesson 9, laid over the **space** part of this lesson. Both are of order $r_s/r$. So why did Lesson 9 say that things fall mainly because of time?

Because a slow object moves very little through space compared with through time. In one second, Earth moves 29.8 km along its orbit, but “moves” 299,792 km along the time axis ($c \times 1$ second). The curvature of time acts on the part of the motion along time; the curvature of space acts only on the part through space. The contribution of space relative to time is of order $(v/c)^2$:

- Earth around the Sun: $(v/c)^2 \approx 10^{-8}$;
- a GPS satellite: $1{,}7 \times 10^{-10}$.

**Light** is different: it moves through space exactly as much as through time ($v = c$). The two parts contribute equally, so light is bent **twice** as much as the time part alone predicts. That is exactly where Einstein in 1911 got only half (about 0.83 arcseconds with his data, 0.87 with today’s) for a ray grazing the Sun (using the closed-box argument of Lesson 7, which sees only the time part), and in 1915 recalculated it as 1.75 arcseconds. Lesson 14 tells the story of measuring it.

[[Color by clock rate|mau]] [[Remove color|khongMau]]

+++ Go deeper: comparing the two parts in the weak-field metric
In a weak field, written in a convenient coordinate system (Hartle, chapter 6), the metric around a mass has the form

$$ \dd s^2 = -\left(1 + \frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\right)c^2\dd t^2 + \left(1 - \frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\right)\left(\dd x^2 + \dd y^2 + \dd z^2\right), \qquad \Phi = -\frac{GM}{r}. $$

The two departures from flatness have the same size $2|\Phi|/c^2$. For an object covering $\dd x = v\,\dd t$:

- the time part is off by $\dfrac{2|\Phi|}{c^2} \cdot c^2\dd t^2$;
- the space part is off by $\dfrac{2|\Phi|}{c^2} \cdot v^2\dd t^2$.

The ratio is exactly $v^2/c^2$. For slow objects only the time part matters, and we recover all of Newtonian mechanics (Lesson 9, last step). For light, $v = c$, the space part contributes exactly as much as the time part. Deflection at the Sun’s limb: the time part alone gives $r_s/R \approx 0{,}875''$, both parts together give $2r_s/R \approx 1{,}75''$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: Clearing up a misconception: the rubber sheet and the marble
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
A familiar picture from books and magazines: a heavy ball presses a dip into a rubber sheet, and a small marble rolls around and falls into the dip. The curved surface in this lesson looks like that, but it differs in three important ways.

1. **It uses gravity to explain gravity.** The marble rolls down into the dip because Earth pulls it down. Take away Earth’s gravity and, however deep the dip in the rubber sheet, the marble will not roll.
2. **There is no “downward.”** The vertical direction of Flamm’s paraboloid is only for drawing. A creature living on the surface can measure only distances along the surface; there is no direction to “roll down.” Put a marble at rest on this surface and the curved space gives it no reason to move.
3. **It leaves out the time part.** A real marble at rest starts to fall because time runs more slowly close to a mass (Lesson 9, Lesson 10). That is the main part of gravity for every slow object, and the rubber sheet does not have it.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Planets orbit the Sun like marbles rolling around the rim of a funnel.” For Earth, curved space contributes only about $10^{-8}$ compared with the time part. The orbit is almost entirely due to curved time.

> [Tóm lại] Curvature around a mass has two parts: time (clocks run slow nearby) and space (rulers measure more than the difference in radii). Slow objects feel almost only the time part; light feels both equally. Lesson 12 puts both together into the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime and Einstein’s equation.

bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.ten: Proper distance in the radial direction
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: $r$ is defined through the circumference $2\pi r$. At $r = 2\,r_s$ the ruler measures 1.414 times $\dd r$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: Taken from the Schwarzschild metric with $\dd t = 0$, $\theta = 90°$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: $z$ is an extra direction used only for drawing. Inside a star of uniform density: a spherical cap of radius $\sqrt{R^3/r_s}$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.ten: Extra length in a weak field
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: Earth, from the ground up to $2R$: 3.1 mm.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: The space part contributes about $(v/c)^2$ relative to the time part: negligible for slow objects, equal for light.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A string is stretched around the Sun far from its surface, and the circumference measures $2\pi \times 10^6$ km. What is the quantity $r$ in this lesson’s formulas at that place?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: Exactly $10^6$ km, because $r$ is defined through circumference
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: Slightly more than $10^6$ km, because space is curved
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: It cannot be known without measuring from the center
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: That is precisely the definition of $r$ (the reduced circumference). What departs from flat geometry is the distance measured in the radial direction, not the circumference.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Around a neutron star of radius 12 km, a ruler is laid from the surface out to the circle of circumference $2\pi \times 24$ km. About what does the ruler read?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The difference in radii is 12 km, plus an extra 1.78 km (about 14.8%). The ruler always reads more, never less, than the difference in radii.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: What is the vertical direction of Flamm’s paraboloid in the picture?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: The third dimension of space (real height)
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: An extra direction used only for drawing, to show the curvature; it is not real
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: The direction in which objects are pulled down
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: The two-dimensional surface is embedded in an imaginary three-dimensional space so that the eye can see the extra length. Only distances measured along the surface are real. Choosing “the direction objects are pulled down” is exactly the trap of the rubber-sheet picture.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why does the curvature of space have almost no effect on Earth’s orbit around the Sun?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Because space around the Sun is not curved
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Because Earth moves very little through space compared with along the time axis; the space part contributes only about $(v/c)^2 \approx 10^{-8}$
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: Because the curvature of space exists only inside the Sun
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: In one second Earth moves 29.8 km through space but 299,792 km along the time axis. The curvature of time acts on the far larger part.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: In 1911 Einstein calculated that a ray grazing the Sun is bent by about 0.87 arcseconds (using today’s data); in 1915 he recalculated it as twice that, 1.75. Where did the extra part come from?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: From the curvature of space, which the closed-box argument cannot see; for light it contributes as much as the time part
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The 1911 argument used only the equivalence principle, that is, the time part. The complete theory adds the space part; light moves at $v = c$, so the two parts are equal.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: A friend says: “Gravity is like a ball pressing a dip into a rubber sheet, and a marble rolling into the dip.” Point out where this is right and where it is wrong.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Right: a mass curves the geometry around it, and the curved surface does look like a dented rubber sheet (Flamm’s paraboloid is the real spatial part of the curvature). Wrong in three ways: (1) the marble rolls because Earth’s gravity pulls it down, which uses gravity to explain gravity; (2) Flamm’s paraboloid has no “downward,” the vertical direction is only for drawing; (3) the picture leaves out the time part, and for slow objects it is the time part that makes things fall and keeps planets in orbit. Curved space only plays a significant role for fast things such as light.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 7: embedding diagrams; chapter 9: the geometry outside a spherical star, radial distances.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: E. F. Taylor, J. A. Wheeler and E. Bertschinger, *Exploring Black Holes* (2nd ed.): ruler distance and “reduced circumference” around a black hole, with embedding diagrams.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: R. P. Feynman, *The Feynman Lectures on Physics*, vol. II, chapter 42 “Curved Space”: two-dimensional curved space, and the “excess radius” around a mass.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: Jonsson 2005, “Visualizing curved spacetime,” Am. J. Phys. 73, 248: why the rubber-sheet picture is misleading, and how to draw the time part too.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: The circumference of a circle around a mass divided by $2\pi$. This is the $r$ in the Schwarzschild metric; it is not equal to the distance measured from the center.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: Distance measured with a ruler at rest right there, on an “all at the same moment” slice. Radially around a mass: $\dd\ell = \dd r/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A way of drawing a curved two-dimensional surface as a surface in an imaginary three-dimensional space, so that distances measured along it are correct. The added direction is only for drawing.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The embedding diagram of the equatorial slice outside a spherical mass: $z = 2\sqrt{r_s(r - r_s)}$. Found by Ludwig Flamm in 1916.
